creator: Bentham's Newsletter
title: Yes, Natural Law Theory is Obviously False
full_text:
Brian Besong, associate professor at Saint Francis University, has written a reply to me on natural law theory.  The piece is peppered with asides and insults—a slightly ironic addition to his extreme reaction to ’s vicious “unprofessional…reputational harm,” which came about when Amos included this jovial Tweet in his article reviewing their debate.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mY1A!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4056aa76-5a60-432e-a62d-80e00182dfe3_828x838.jpeg]]

I find it odd to treat that light poking as such a vicious personal slight that it demands derailing a debate about natural law theory into a several minute long grievance-fest about the vicious “reputational harm” you suffered, while having your response to a relatively neutral post be densely layered with insults.1  It is also odd to take offense at someone using your first name but to claim that the other person is ignorant, very online, hasn’t read much about natural law theory, unoriginal, etc.  One senses a lack of consistency.  But anyways, I will avoid getting into a mudslinging contest with Besong and just respond to his arguments.

Besong claims that my piece with “the sort of enthusiasm typical of the Very Online, concluded that [natural law] theory is ‘obviously false.’”  This judgment is not mine alone, of course.  It is shared by virtually every philosopher in the world.  I will also note that it isn’t as if I don’t go around saying every view I disagree with is obviously false; that is a judgment I make rarely, only in cases where views are really truly implausible.  NLT fits the bill.

Besong then complains that I engage no natural law scholarship and that my objections are not particularly original.  That is true.  Sometimes, if you are explaining the core reasons to reject a view, you will primarily cite standard pre-existing arguments rather than cite cutting edge scholarship.  When  wrote his piece on utilitarianism, he did not cite much utilitarian scholarship and his objections were not original.  Nonetheless, it was a serious piece—so serious that back in the day, I wrote a ten part reply to it.

One gets the sense that his knowledge of natural law comes almost exclusively from watching my debate with Dustin Crummett, and a few odd things picked up elsewhere on the internet. The impression he gives, by leaving out literally any argument natural lawyers have given for their views, is that this is a quirky view held uniquely by Catholics, incapable of even the slightest philosophical scrutiny.

Perhaps this is the sense that Besong has gotten, but it isn’t accurate.  I have spent a reasonable amount of time engaging with natural law (for example, as Besong is aware, I participated in at least one debate on the subject).  It isn’t true that I left “out literally any argument natural lawyers have given for their views.”  I am puzzled that Besong thinks that because he spends a considerable portion of his essay criticizing my reply to his argument for natural law theory.  I do agree, however, that NLT does not survive even the slightest philosophical scrutiny.

No doubt that is what Adelstein thinks, which is why his blog post is so philosophically sloppy. While this is no place to rehash all of those arguments, I would point to the last chapter of my recent Sex in Theory as comprising a strong argument for natural law as yet unchallenged: namely, it is the only extant moral theory capable of explaining Moorean truths about the bedroom. While Adelstein takes issue with how natural law explains those truths—points I will address below—the omission of a genuine rival explanation is telling.

Again, this isn’t true.  I discussed two different explanations: one involved biting the bullet and rejecting these supposed “Moorean” truths and the other about the wrong kinds of relationships.  I am also puzzled that Besong thinks that I left his argument “as yet unchallenged” while also complaining about the responses I gave to it.  I also have no idea how a person could have read my post and come away thinking that I did not give a genuine rival explanation; Besong discusses the rival explanation.  What did he think he was doing?

Adelstein’s objections have the twin defects of being bad and unoriginal. Were it not for the fact that I’m named outright—even by first name, as though we were old pals—I’d ignore them. As it is, I’ll deal with them swiftly.

I agree that they are by and large unoriginal.  No need to reinvent the wheel!  As for Besong taking offense to my using his first name, I was not aware that this is the sort of thing he’d take offense to.  I also referred to Dustin Crummett as Dustin.  I think it’s a pretty normal thing for a Ph.D. student to refer to a professor by their first name.

Besong discusses my egoism objection to NLT: NLT is egoistic.  It says your reasons to help others is for the sake of your own happiness.  Others’ happiness is only the source of reasons because it improves your own.  Besong admits that the view is egoistic, however, he thinks that this is not a bad result.  He writes:

Adelstein appeals to an intuition I don’t share: “this gets the order of explanation wrong.” And worse, he makes a claim that favors my view in its defense: “Part of why you should help other people is for their sake.” Part. Yeah, I agree. As a social being, caring for others “for their sake” is part of my nature, a nature I should not ignore. It’s a part of the explanation.

I’m not sure that there’s that much I can say if you just don’t share the intuition.  But let me give it a try.  Imagine a view says that helping others is only right because it is good for you to help others—a kind of objective list theory egoism on which helping others is on the list.  Even though this would give you reason to help others, it would incorrectly explain why you should help others.  It would say that you should do it only because doing so is good for you, rather than for their sake.

On Besong’s view, helping someone else is only good because it contributes to your happiness.  If something else contributed equally to your happiness, construed broadly, it would be just as good for you to do.  This doesn’t seem right and I expect most people to share my intuition here.

Besong then suggests that there is a very powerful argument for egoism that I didn’t respond to.  It is true that I did not respond to it, just as I didn’t respond to a lot of arguments given by NLTists—one cannot respond to every objection in a single blog post.

Here is the challenge: egoism is supposed to explain why morality has genuinely binding and authoritative force.  An amoralist might wonder: why should I be moral?  The egoist has an answer: because doing so is good for you.  He complains that others have to “develop a notion of reasons that, to reapply a phrase from J.L. Mackie, are ‘queer.’”

I don’t see this as much of a challenge.  Why should you do what’s right?  This is analytic.  The word “right” just refers to what you should do!  The realist thinks there  are facts about what you should do.  I’m not sure why these facts are supposed to be any more queer than the modal, mathematical, or logical facts.

But it’s also not clear how NLT is supposed to help.  Suppose I don’t care about my good.  I only care about, say, my present good or my good on Tuesdays.  How does NLT explain why I should do what’s right?  Besong suggests that “moral reasons are always deeply connected to what each individual necessarily cares about,” but I don’t see how this can be right.  I certainly don’t care about my proper functioning.  If I learned that something impeded my proper function, I just wouldn’t care in the slightest.

Or suppose that, like most people, I care intrinsically about other people’s happiness rather than just my own.  Why should I do what’s good for my happiness, rather than the happiness of others?  What answer does the egoist have for the person who cares about more than their own happiness?

Adelstein quickly moves to safe territory: highlighting a counterintuitive implication of natural law, hoping that it supplies force to his second premise. For he’s right to say that, on natural law, one should not lie to save one’s family from torture. The problem here is that the argument should be an obvious sleight of hand. Ethical egoism is a matter of explaining ultimate (moral) reasons. It does not tell us anything about what the moral norms are. Here Adelstein’s real objection is to the moral norm, not the explanation of reasons.

I think Besong misunderstands my point.  The reason I suggested this was an objection to NLT’s egoism was that NLT implies that the reason you shouldn’t lie to prevent your family from being tortured to death is that it would be bad for your happiness.  But intuitively, even if somehow that is bad for your happiness, it seems you should do it anyways.  You should take a small hit to your happiness so that your family isn’t tortured to death.

Besong then objects to utilitarianism on grounds that it implies that you should torture a young girl in order to prevent a sufficiently large number of people from undergoing intense suffering.  I agree with this judgment.  I think the main reason it’s counterintuitive is that we naturally think preventing lots of mild harms isn’t as good as preventing a big harm.  It isn’t extremely intuitive that torturing one person to stop everyone from being tortured would be wrong.  In fact, I think there are pretty decisive arguments that doing so would be right.

So then the strangeness of the judgment comes down to whether preventing a lot of little harms is as good as preventing one big harm.  I think it is and I’ve defended that here and here.  I agree that this is counterintuitive but I don’t think our intuitions about big numbers are very trustworthy and, in addition, there are very strong arguments for thinking that some number of mild harms are worse than one very grave harm.

But if you reject that judgment, fine, don’t be an aggregationist.  Still, that would supply little reason to be an NLTist.

Both utilitarianism and NLT are counterintuitive sometimes.  The difference is that we can give strong arguments for the utilitarian verdicts, strong debunkings of the non-utilitarian verdicts, and the judgments, while sounding bad, become less obviously wrong when you think about them.  If you really imagine that your action prevents an infinite amount of badness—preventing infinite people from suffering mildly—it no longer seems so obvious that you shouldn’t do it.

Besong then responds to my argument that goodness and proper functioning can come apart.  If a pill increased your happiness but didn’t positively contribute to your functioning, it would be good for you.

Gestures toward independent support of the premise supply the rest: a joy pill, say, which is supposed to be good for me (how? Experience machine, anyone?) despite being unrelated to proper function (why not?)

Taking the pill would do something in your brain that makes you feel more pleasant experiences but doesn’t enhance your proper functioning.  This is not like the experience machine because it increases your joy without destroying all the non-hedonic value in your life.

He then responds to my argument that we can imagine a creature with a very bad proper function.  For example, maybe a being would properly function by causing torment and misery.  He suggests these are impossible because God would never make such creatures.  It’s not clear that it actually is impossible.  It might even be actual.  There are some animals that lay eggs in the skin of other animals to reproduce.  Their proper functioning involves doing very horrible things.

But anyways, even if God would never make it, it can still be a counterexample.  I’ll just repeat what I said in the post:

Now, maybe the reply would be that God would never create such a creature. But still, a true ethical theory should get the right results in cases that God could choose to actualize if he wanted to, even if he would never choose to actualize it.

Imagine there was a theory that said that it would be okay to press a button that would cause everyone to be tortured for all of eternity. That example would obviously falsify the theory. Nobody would buy the reply “that’s an impossible scenario because God would never choose to actualize it.” There are some scenarios that are impossible but still serve as counterexamples. I don’t have a complete theory of which scenarios are like that. But certainly at the very least, a theory can be falsified by getting a wrong result in one of the scenarios that God could create if he wanted to but never would choose to create because they’re too bad.

Besong replies:

And if impossible worlds can serve as counterexamples to a normative theory, then my coherently conceiving of a world in which suffering is intrinsically good refutes his preferred consequentialism.

But I obviously don’t think that the fact that you can imagine an impossible world where a theory is false suffices to refute it.  Working out the details of counterpossibles is tricky.  Still, as the examples above show, there are clearly some cases where a counterpossible can be a genuine counterexample.  I don’t have a complete theory of these, as I said, but I gave one class of possible conditions: if there is a world that is only impossible because God would never choose to create it, though he could if he wanted to, it still suffices as a genuine counterexample.  I thought this  was pretty clear in my essay.  Besong doesn’t address it.

Besong also ignores the following example:

Then, lastly, it seems that there can be a giant group of creatures functioning improperly. Imagine that a plague swept through humans, causing all of our eyes to be destroyed. In a few generations, we had no eyes. Still, a properly functioning human would have eyes. Thus, it is possible for all members of a species not to be functioning properly.

But now imagine we learned that actual humans were this way. Our proper function was to be solitary animals who spend our days without clothes, rolling around in the mud. Still, that wouldn’t seem to be good for us. Thus, what’s good for a person isn’t the same as proper functioning.

Besong must agree that it’s possible for most people to engage in improper function.  After all, he thinks this is what most people do with respect to sex and lying.  Most people have sex outside the bounds of wedlock and sometimes lie.  So then he cannot object to this example on grounds that it’s too horrific for God to actualize; it’s not particularly horrific.  God has made solitary creatures.  It’s not clear why it’s inconceivable that God makes creatures who are solitary by nature but enjoy the company of others, just like he makes creatures who are oriented towards procreation by nature but enjoy non-procreative intercourse.

My next argument is that it is obviously permissible to misuse faculties sometimes.  If the only way to stop the holocaust was to lie about what you’d had for breakfast, that would obviously be permissible.  Besong just bites the bullet here.  The reader is free to consult their own intuitions to see if this seems plausible to them.  To me, it seems vastly less plausible than almost anything I can imagine.

Adelstein later supports premise two independently, by talking about slight misuses for the sake of overall flourishing (or functioning), but this assumes a maximizing view of happiness that’s simply mistaken (and not just because Adelstein repeatedly conflates happiness for subjective feelings).

Besong gave zero examples of this conflation, despite its supposed “repeated” occurrence.

I find it unclear why, if one is only concerned about their own happiness, they can’t cause themselves unhappiness for greater future happiness.  Note that I am not saying that natural law theorists think this.  I agree they think it’s wrong to misuse a faculty even to prevent future misuse.  But I am not sure why they think this.  If you were concerned about your own happiness, I would imagine that you would care equally about your happiness at each moment of your life.

For NLT to be plausible, it must explain why you can’t misuse a faculty to prevent future misuse.  Noting that the view thinks that isn’t an explanation of the verdict.

If natural law were committed to such a view, it would also support Life Support Larry, who realizes that saving people close to death best expresses his inner virtues and drives, and so (while in the ICU) allows patients to get dangerously close to death so that he can save them. Life Support Larry does not understand genuine human flourishing, and apparently, he’s not alone. Adelstein is importing consequentialist analyses where they are deeply unwanted.

But presumably Besong doesn’t think that a person would actually flourish more, in total, if they allow patients to get dangerously close to death and save them while they’re on the brink of death.  Maybe he does think that.  But if he does and NLT in conjunction with thinking that you can misuse a faculty for the sake of greater future use leads to this result, then all the worse for NLT!  Note that pointing out that the view would suck if you onboarded some plausible assumption is not an explanation of why the assumption is wrong.

Maybe the objection wasn’t clear.  So let me lay it out as clearly as I can: imagine that you were only concerned with your own happiness.  You’d be able to do things that make you unhappy for the sake of future happiness.  So then why, if happiness is about flourishing, can’t you cause yourself present improper function to improve aggregate proper function?

My next objection is that NLT struggles to explain why homosexuality, say, is impermissible but chewing a plastic straw, drinking a drink with no nutritional value, and listening to noise-cancelling headphones are permissible.

I’ll be brief: noise cancelling headphones, like antiperspirant, do not use a power against its own end. Hearing is not a sound-input-maximizing power, nor is the normothermic system a sweat-maximizing power. These are red herrings (and one would know as much if one read recent papers by, say, John Skalko or Tim Hsiao, among others)

…

Both licking a stamp and chewing a straw are superfluous uses of a constitutive power whose proximate goals have not been frustrated (the power to salivate and masticate, respectively). Confusion arises centrally when one conflates the proximate end of these “constitutive” subpowers with the end of the integral power which it subserves: for both salivation and mastication, the integral end is health (via digestion). A parallel in sexual acts is not open, since these are aimed at conception, and ultimately procreation.

I have not read the paper, so I’ll just briefly respond to this suggestion.  Presumably the proper function of sweating is cooling yourself down and the proper functioning of salivation is digestion.  Now, if you chew gum, this doesn’t actually subvert your digestion—it isn’t as though your digestion is worse.  But similarly, if you have non-procreative sex, it isn’t as though your probability of procreation goes down.  So this doesn’t establish an asymmetry.

Similarly, I don’t think this helps much with the noise-cancelling headphones example.  They block noise, rather than just fail to maximize sound.  When you have them in, you can’t hear.  So why isn’t wearing them wrong?

Next Besong discusses a case that  originally gave of—it turns out hypothetical—frat guys who fellate each other in order to learn what it’s like.  It’s unclear how this is supposed to differ from chewing gum.  Their aim, in this case, is not to use the sexual faculty directly.  Besong says:

Wollen’s gay frat guys case assumes—quite strangely, to my mind—that intent fully dictates the nature of one’s act and that intent is fully determined by what people tell themselves (or others) about their actions. Both of those are deeply problematic in their own right, and I could find no better illustration of the problems with both theses than the case Wollen and then Adelstein raise. Were it not disgusting in its depravity, I would be delighted they keep pressing it. I believe the kids call that a self-own.

It doesn’t assume that.  Besong’s explanation, in his back and forth with Amos, about why it was okay to chew gum was that you’re really exercising the power of chewing.  That power is broadly oriented towards some other end, and it’s not being used improperly.  But similarly, Amos argued that if a person has sex to learn what their partner feels like from the inside, then they’re correctly using their faculty of touch.  None of this requires that intent is determined by what people say!  What we want is a principled asymmetry between the two cases.

Besong’s main argument for natural law theory is that it’s supposed to be the only way to explain Moorean judgments about the absolute wrongness of sex acts.  Pedophilia, incest, necrophilia, etc are all supposed to be explainable by the fact that these are non-procreative.  My reply: this explanation fails because even if these acts were procreative, they’d still be wrong.  It would be worse to have sex with children if it was likely to lead to pregnancy.  Besong objects:

Natural law agrees: kids are too emotionally and psychologically immature to raise children or consent to marriage, the relationship in which sex is rightfully constrained.

But obviously we can imagine a bunch of cases where that’s not true.  Imagine that if you had sex with a child, they would only become pregnant much later—at the time when they’d be a good parent.  Seems that in such a case, Besong’s view can’t explain why such an action would be wrong.  Or at least, if it can, then whatever he uses to explain it isn’t constitutively procreation-related, so I can explain it that way too!

Adelstein suggests also that sex with animals would be wrong even if it were procreative. Presumably not with humanoid, rational Martians. But even if we could birth rational children with some brute beast—and in this case, I’m not sure how strong our intuitions of wrongness would be—a brute beast is also psychologically incapable of acting as the parent of a rational agent. Again, marriage, whose objective constraints require rational commitments, is out in such a case, hence the sex is wrong.

Imagine that a man is married to an infertile woman.  He could, with her permission, have sex with an animal that was mentally like a dog but capable of giving birth to fully human babies.  How does Besong explain the intrinsic wrongness of such an act?

Lastly, he thinks that as the rates of genetic problems between token individuals could compare or exceed the genetic problems of incest as a type of act, so both stand or fall together. The problem is that natural law is a theory about human nature, a type rather than a token. While we must care about token effects of our token actions, they do not ground judgments about the intrinsic teleology of act types. Once more Adelstein is smuggling in consequentialism. (It should come as little surprise to the reader that much of this is discussed at length in Sex in Theory, a book Adelstein appears unfamiliar with.)

So let me get this straight: the way one determines the categories of acts is so discriminatory that sex within marriage is supposed to be distinguished from sex outside of marriage with respect to their tendency towards procreation.  It also differentiates sex with the very young from sex with those of standard child-bearing age.  But it doesn’t differentiate between sex with those in childbearing age and those above childbearing age?  Why could this be?  And appealing to a type/token distinction is of no help, because all these things are both a type and a token—a token instance of some more general type, but also conceivably a type in themselves.

What is the explanation of why having sex with a family member is to be treated as a non-procreative act type but having sex with someone above the age of 40 or an infertile person is not?  Being snarky is no answer to this question.  Having now read the section of Sex in Theory on this question, I do not find it to provide an explanation of the distinction—it does little more than gesture in the direction of the type/token distinction and explain that you should evaluate kinds of acts.  It does not explain why there is a distinction.

Finally, Besong addresses my two accounts of the permissibility of incest, necrophilia, bestiality, etc.  I think he is confused and thinks these two accounts are just one account.  But they are not.

The first account involves biting the bullet and saying that these acts are horrible in approximately all real world cases but if we imagine a case where the involved parties don’t suffer at all, have a good time, face no long-term psychological damage, feel no regret, etc, then they wouldn’t be wrong.  He suggests it’s just obvious that these kinds of acts are impermissible.

Is it obvious?  I don’t really think so.  If I imagine these acts, while they seem reckless and like bad ideas, if we imagine they produce no untoward suffering, it doesn’t seem obvious to me that they’re wrong.  I think our intuitions might be infected by the fact that these acts are generally wrong, so we overgeneralize.

To take a specific example: in Orson Scott Card’s Speaker For the Dead, two of the characters who are lovers later learn that they’re siblings.  Imagine that they had never learned this.  They had two happy and healthy children.  They went to their deaths madly in love.  Then imagine a historian turned out this fact a hundred years later.  Would this have made their love tragic?  Would it be better for it never to have been?  Doesn’t seem obvious to me!  Certainly doesn’t seem Moorean.  If no one suffers, who is supposed to be wronged?

Then I gave a second account according to which sex is only proper between rational beings with the right kinds of relationships.  I don’t think this account is terribly ad hoc.  It’s standard to think that relationships are of intrinsic moral importance, so if sex perverts a relationship that should be non-sexual, it’s wrong.  Similarly, it’s natural to think that having sex with a non-rational creature—an animal, say—would be wrong.

What he gives is not a philosophical account of the morality of the bedroom but an ad hoc checklist: “it’s only okay to have sex when every involved party is suitably rational and doing so wouldn’t pervert any relationship that ought to be non-sexual.” How rational and why? Which relationships, and why? Ironically, he immediately follows with openness to incest, bestiality, and necrophilia being permissible. If we’re going to talk about things that are obviously false, Adelstein should start with theories open to that.

The only one I had in mind was a familial relationship.  Maybe there are others; it might be immoral to have sex with your friend’s mom (I will refrain from making the obvious joke).  I don’t know the exact threshold of rationality, but presumably it would lie somewhere around the legal threshold for age of consent.  Presumably Besong also thinks that there’s some threshold of rationality—it would be wrong for me to marry and sleep with someone with the mind of a young child.  So this is everyone’s problem.

Note that this account rules out bestiality, incest, and necrophilia (corpses aren’t rational, animals aren’t rational, and incest perverts a relationship that should be non-sexual).  So it isn’t right that these supposedly Moorean judgments are counterexamples, even if one truly finds them Moorean.  Now, Besong has some questions about this account—I don’t find them very challenging to answer, but in any case, they’re certainly less tortured than the NLTists explanations.

In conclusion then, I do not find any of Besong’s replies to be successful.   NLT remains very implausible.  If he wants to have another debate on this subject, I’d be up for it.

1You might object that my post called his view obviously false.  But describing a view as obviously wrong isn’t the same sort of thing as repeatedly insulting the author of the view.  Now, I don’t mind—I find a little bit of rhetorical viciousness in blog posts a delightful thing—but it is odd to combine it with the delicate sensibilities displayed by Besong in his debate with Amos.

notes.note: Natural law ethics has contemporary philosophical defenders. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy lists defenders including Germain Grisez, John Finnis, Alasdair MacIntyre, Mark Murphy, Michael Moore, Philippa Foot and Michael Thompson.
